faqs.q: I found a raccoon in my Lancaster attic — can you move it to the woods?
faqs.a: We do not promise that, because South Carolina does not allow it: SCDNR states that routine relocation of wildlife is against state law, and a captured animal must be destroyed or, with a separate department permit, may be relocated. What our crew does is eviction and exclusion — the raccoon leaves through a one-way door or is removed under SCDNR depredation rules, and then we seal every entry in steel so the attic stays closed. Raccoons are also South Carolina's leading rabies carrier in the Department of Public Health's testing, so attic latrines get cleaned and sanitized, not just emptied.

faqs.q: There is a dead animal smell in my Lancaster walls. What should I do?
faqs.a: Call us rather than opening walls at random. Our crew locates the carcass — a dead raccoon, opossum, or squirrel in a wall void or crawlspace is the usual source — removes it, and sanitizes the area. Carcasses of raccoons, skunks, and bats are handled with rabies precautions in line with Department of Public Health guidance, and we check how the animal got in so the entry is sealed as part of the same visit.

Kershaw is a Lancaster County town with gold in its ground — the Haile Gold Mine outside town has been worked since the 1820s and still shapes the local landscape of pits, ponds, and timbered company land. The town itself is classic upcountry South Carolina: older homes along tree-lined streets, churches, a small downtown, and farmland and pine woods at every edge. Its wildlife work is that setting's: raccoons and bats in the older homes, gray squirrels in the street canopy, groundhogs in the field banks, and the creeks — Lynch's River country to the east — carrying beaver work to the low properties.

Kershaw's quiet is part of the pattern. A small town with a large retired and working-from-home population has houses that stand undisturbed for long stretches of the day and, for some owners, long stretches of the year — and undisturbed is what attic animals are shopping for. Our Kershaw inspections assume a quiet older home has been prospected until the read proves it clean, and they document everything for owners who may be reviewing the report from somewhere else.
Kershaw.extendedBody:
Mine land, timber land, and the town between

Kershaw's surroundings are unusual even for the upcountry: thousands of acres of mine and timber holdings stand around the town as managed wild ground, and the wildlife population they hold commutes the town's edges nightly. Boundary properties get the full ground pass — banks, branches, and burrows — with the building read. Groundhogs hold the sunny banks along the farm roads; beavers work the creek branches in the wet years; and the deer-lease woods keep a raccoon population that discovers every uncapped chimney in town on a multi-year rotation. Sealing, here as everywhere, is the permanent line item: the permit removes today's animal, the metal refuses tomorrow's.

How removal is authorized in South Carolina

There is no SCDNR operator license in this state — a referral list only — so weigh any company's credential claims accordingly. Our Kershaw work runs on the depredation permit for your property under §50-11-2570(A), naming the species, with the state's handling rules attached: bats excluded by SCDNR's timing guidance (never sealed in while pups are flightless), rabies-suspect animals reported through SC DPH, beaver on the year-long permit. That framework, explained plainly, is the substance to judge an operator by.

The older home, read completely

Kershaw's pre-war homes carry the familiar list — open eaves, layered junctions, unscreened crawlspaces — and the town's big street trees bridge to most of them. We map the entries, exclude the residents, and seal in metal fitted to old framing. In a small town, the work is also its own reference: the houses that stay sealed stay quiet, and the neighbours notice both kinds.
